title: The Courtroom
acts: Day nine of the trial, and the county courthouse had long since stopped pretending to be dignified. Arthur — eighty if he was a day, robed, red tie knotted like a threat, half-moon spectacles polished to a shine — had abandoned the judge's bench entirely and was standing out on the open floor in front of it, gavel raised, taking practice swings at nothing. The potted plant beside him had learned to flinch. "I want it on the record," he announced to a stenographer who had gone home on Tuesday, "that this is the finest gavel arm in the state."

Over on the prosecution side, Daisy had claimed the carpet as sovereign territory. Platinum bun, purple spectacles, closing argument delivered at full volume to a jury box containing one abandoned cardigan — she paced that rug end to end and would not step off it, on the grounds that stepping off it would concede something. Howard, who had white hair, a white moustache and a tan jacket the colour of weak tea, had been sheltering behind the same potted plant since the lunch recess, waiting to be called as an expert on something he had privately forgotten. He whispered his credentials to the plant. The plant took no view. Meanwhile, at the witness stand, Eliza stood on the carpet in her pearls, forty minutes into an answer to the question "and what time was that?", showing no sign of nearing the verb.

In the gallery, the public had thinned to two. Camila, ponytail high, lilac top, had queued since six in the morning and was now the only living soul in the building with an actual seat, which she defended with a flask and an expression. Benjamin, black-framed glasses, navy suit, remained on his feet at the far end of the row of chairs, having objected eleven times from the public benches without any standing whatsoever, glaring across the gallery at the seated woman with the flask. And in the security room, Graham — bald, neat goatee, uniform shirt straining — sat beside a bank of monitors with his boots up, watching a nature documentary on one of them. So nobody, anywhere in that building, was watching when a noise went off like a wardrobe falling down a lift shaft, and Vanessa stopped filing her notes forever.

whereabouts.A: Arthur, robed and half-moon-spectacled, had stepped down onto the open floor in front of the Judge's Bench to rehearse his gavel swing beside the long bench table, a chair and one thoroughly intimidated plant.
whereabouts.B: Benjamin, in his navy suit and heavy black glasses, was up on his feet at the end of a row of Gallery chairs, objecting to proceedings he had no part in and resenting the one person in the room who'd got a seat.
whereabouts.C: Camila, ponytail and lilac top, was parked in the only occupied chair in the Gallery, having queued since dawn to secure it, and had no intention of vacating it for anybody.
whereabouts.D: Daisy, platinum bun and purple spectacles, was delivering her Prosecution closing while pacing the carpet she was standing on, refusing on principle to set foot off it, with the prosecution table and its chairs as her long-suffering audience.
whereabouts.E: Eliza, blonde bob and pearls, stood sworn in on the carpet of the Witness Stand beside its rail table, extending a single answer past the forty-minute mark in the hope of never being cross-examined.
whereabouts.F: Fritz, young and navy-suited and unnervingly blank of face, was second chair on the Defense side, standing on open floor at one end of the enormous table and quietly working out exactly how heavy it was.
whereabouts.G: Graham, bald with a trim goatee and a straining uniform shirt, was in the Security area beside the TV, watching wildebeest instead of the camera feeds he was paid to watch.
whereabouts.H: Howard, white-moustached in a tan jacket, was lurking in the Prosecution corner beside the potted plant, rehearsing his expert credentials to its leaves while he waited to be called.
whereabouts.V: Vanessa, dark-haired and bespectacled in her black blazer, was lead counsel on the Defense side, standing on open floor at the far end of the room with her back to it all, sorting notes for an afternoon session she never got.

reveal: It was Fritz, in the Defense area, with the table. He had spent nine days being called "and associate" while Vanessa took the podium, the credit and the good chair, and something in him simply filed a motion. Standing on the open floor at the near end of the room, he got both hands under the edge of that vast slab of courtroom oak, shouted "OBJECTION!" purely for the acoustics, and heaved. The table went up on one edge, hung there for a beautiful cartoon moment, and then came down the length of the room like a felled redwood — flat, final, and roughly the shape of a very large pressed flower. Arthur's gavel arm never got its moment. The table got it instead.

escape.generic: The jury box stayed empty, the case went in a drawer marked 'later', and somewhere out there a young lawyer is telling the story at parties and calling it a workplace accident.

byAccused.A: They led Arthur out still holding the gavel, swinging it at the ceiling and demanding to preside over his own arrest — while the actual culprit held the door open for him, very politely.
byAccused.B: Benjamin was hauled off mid-objection, which he took as vindication that he'd had standing all along, and the person who really did it never so much as raised a hand.
byAccused.C: Camila was arrested in her chair, refused to stand, and had to be carried out seat and all — she'd queued since six for that view and got a cell instead, while the guilty party strolled home.
byAccused.D: Daisy was charged on her own carpet, mid-sentence, and went down insisting she'd never once stepped off it — which was true, and which the real killer found extremely convenient.
byAccused.E: Eliza was taken into custody still finishing an answer about what time it was, and the person who should have been in those cuffs slipped out somewhere around the twelfth minute.
byAccused.G: Graham was done for it on the strength of having watched nothing at all, which is not evidence, but the tapes agreed with him and the real culprit walked out past every camera he wasn't watching.
byAccused.H: Howard was marched away from his plant protesting that he was an expert witness, and never did remember in what — meanwhile the guilty party was already outside, ordering lunch.
